lesson_title: One Rand, Many Pockets: the Multiplier
hook_text: Government pays a road crew R1 000. The town ends up R5 000 richer. Here's how.
clip_script: Government fixes the road through a small town and pays a local crew one thousand rand. Watch that thousand. The bricklayer keeps two hundred for school fees and spends eight hundred — meat, mielie meal, paraffin, taxi fare. That eight hundred is now the spaza owner's income. He keeps a fifth and spends six hundred and forty restocking. The wholesaler keeps a fifth and spends five hundred and twelve. Count the people paid from ONE payment: bricklayer, spaza owner, wholesaler, helper, tavern owner, barber. Add the whole chain and the town's income rose by five thousand rand — five times the original thousand. That's the multiplier. But here's the catch, and it's the exam's favourite. At every stop, a slice steps out. Some gets saved. Some goes in tax. And some buys something IMPORTED — that money leaves the country and never becomes anybody's income here again. If half of every rand steps out each round, your thousand adds two thousand, not five. Same road, same wage, half the effect. Which is why WHO gets the money and WHAT it buys decide how far it travels.
visual_style: A single R100 note travelling a dusty main street, splitting at each shopfront: a slice peeling off into a bank book, a tax stamp and an aeroplane, the remainder shrinking but moving on.
pacing: Fast hand-offs through the six pockets, a hard stop at the leak, steady close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and calculate any multiplier — forwards or backwards — in one line.
